answers.question: If you were a freshman at MIT again and knew you wanted to go into this industry, what would you do differently over the next three years?
answers.answer:
1) Don't worry about MCG (I got rejected not 1, but 2 times)
2) Management/business classes are not necessary to be successful in consulting. They care more that you can think critically (which all your STEM classes teach you to do)
3) You don't need the best at anything to land the job. Just make an interesting story about your life and what you do! (MISTI is really helpful)

answers.question: What classes were the most important for industry work? Were any classes really important in terms of appearing on your resume?
answers.answer: No! Do not worry about classes. Management consulting LOVES engineers/really STEM people because they are able to break down problems in a unique way. Anyone can learn management/business on the spot, but teaching someone to problem solve is much more difficult (and I think MIT is a great school to learn how to solve really hard problems). I do think classes that let you work on teams in stressful situations are helpful for two reasons. One, the job feels a lot like that - you are with a group of people working towards a common goal in a high-pressure situation. Two, consulting firms care a lot about your "story" and how you communicate it. Teamwork in these classes can give you good content to talk about in these interview.

answers.question: What did you do during college that actually mattered in getting your first job, and what ended up not mattering as much as you thought it would?
answers.answer:
Helpful: 1) MISTI - I used this as much as possible in my behaviorals (talking about how I had to learn so much (culturally, technically, and socially) in such a condensed timeline. I had an interviewer that told someone mid-interview that they were passing me to the next round regardless of how bad my casing was because they loved my MISTI story so much. So trust...it's awesome to talk about.
2) Few but strong connections - Making a few meaningful connections at companies I was interested in (with as senior people as possible). Leverage MIT...MIT alums LOVE talking to MIT students. 
3) Case prepping buddies - I believe case prep is a matter of practice (and if you are at MIT, you are MORE than capable :)!!!). Here is the progression I used: 1) Start by working through a case prep book - I recommend "Case in Point", 2) Case alone. You will probs be bad unless you're randomly a case god. I wasn't lol. 3) Start to case with low pressure people (friends in your class, me!!!), 4) Case with MIT/APhi alums currently at these companies (reach out)
Didn't matter: Management/biz classes, coffee chatting with 10000 people

answers.question: Were there any clubs that bolstered your resume, helped you make important connections, or really enhanced your knowledge about the industry?
answers.answer: Honestly no - Leverage APhi connections, your sport if you're in one

answers.question: What experiences should I prioritize before I start applying for internships? Like classes, research, clubs, personal projects, internships, leadership, networking, etc.
answers.answer:
I think this is where there is no good answer. I think what you should do as much possible in an area you are passionate in, then make a good story about it that somehow leads you to consulting.
Mine: I have always loved physics, math --> MIT. Wanted to know how things work and learn more in my favorite subjects --> MechE. Wanted to learn more about power resilience and accessibility to reliable power --> Terrascope FY learned about power resilience in PR. Wanted industry experience in the energy space --> Calpine. Loved working with a team, solving a problem, and energy --> Solar research at MIT Renewable Energy Clinic. Wanted a global experience in the power industry --> Interned at Scottish Power. Decided I didn't love the energy industry that much, wanted to be in a team, wanted to jump from industry to industry, wanted to move quick, wasn't in love with the idea of technical work forever, liked seeing big pic strategy --> consulting interest!

answers.question: For someone from MIT, what opportunities or resources do you think I should take advantage of that students often overlook?
answers.answer: Terrascope and MISTI

answers.question: What does a really strong candidate for an internship in your industry look like?
answers.answer: Someone who can both 1) Solve problems well/think quickly on their feet and 2) Communicate your answer well/get along with teammates/pass "The Airport Test"

answers.question: What skills are actually important once you're working in the industry versus skills that are mostly useful for getting through the interview process?
answers.answer:
Interview: Really strong communication, Math on the spot
In-Job: Use AI well LOL, Think quickly and strong communication

answers.question: How did you get your first real opportunity in the industry?
answers.answer: Internship with McKinsey

answers.question: When should I start recruiting, and what does the recruiting timeline look like for internships and full-time roles?
answers.answer: Internship: Now recruiting is really early (around April/May the year before), not sure exact dates but you should have done a decent amount of case prepping before applying but don't need to be great yet (around 4 weeks to hear back about R1 depending on firm); also, diff firms look for diff things....I didn't get an interview at BCG so don't get down on yourself

answers.question: Are there particular companies, roles, or types of internships you think are especially good starting points?
answers.answer: I think management consulting (Bain, BCG, McK). More technical consulting (Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, EY)

answers.question: Are there mistakes you see some students make when trying to break into this industry?
answers.answer: Not case prepping enough, not caring enough about behavioral (big emphasis!!), spending too much time coffee chatting (Who knows how much this matters...)

answers.question: How would you recommend I spend my freshman summer if my ultimate goal is to end up in this field?
answers.answer: Do something interesting! You can get to consulting HOWEVER. I interned in Houston at a mid-sized power company...so it can really be whatever. Industry not important, only how you tell the story.

answers.question: Should I go to the career fair as a freshman? If so, how should I prepare? If not, should I, and what years?
answers.answer: Eh no. I don't know what the career fair does for you lol. Go to explore different careers/industries? I know MIT has consulting events (and I think they do put your name down if you go, so try and attend), but I really think they are to try and sell you on the company/tell you more and aren't a test

answers.question: How important are GPA, major, coursework, extracurriculars, projects, and previous internships when companies are evaluating students?
answers.answer: GPA: I think there is a minimum you have to pass, but MIT carries a lot of weight; Major: They love STEM majors, but really anything goes...; Coursework: Nah; Others: Again, do stuff you care about and tell a cool story!

answers.question: Was there anyone at MIT, like a professor, alum, organization, or career resource, who was particularly helpful to you?
answers.answer: APhi Alums (Sydney Pyon, Megan Eberts, Older APhi Alums) gave very candid advice and were so helpful!

answers.question: If you were a freshman at MIT again and knew you wanted to go into this industry, what would you do differently over the next three years?
answers.answer: Do more cool stuff at MIT that isn't related to finance (e.g., a more serious UROP). + Do mock interviews before recruiting season

answers.question: What classes were the most important for industry work? Were any classes really important in terms of appearing on your resume?
answers.answer: 15.401, 15.501, and 15.402. Don't think any were super necessary to have on a resume but the content was helpful for interview prep

answers.question: What did you do during college that actually mattered in getting your first job, and what ended up not mattering as much as you thought it would?
answers.answer: Very important to talk to upperclassmen and recent alums about their career journeys so far because they will make you aware of opportunities that you wouldn't have known about otherwise (e.g., the Girls Who Invest program). Having connections in the industry was not 100% necessary (you will get interviews for places you don't network at).

answers.question: Were there any clubs that bolstered your resume, helped you make important connections, or really enhanced your knowledge about the industry?
answers.answer: Women Business Leaders was excellent for making connections and getting career advice. Scholars of Finance was also helpful in a similar way. And of course the APhi upperclassmen and recent alums

answers.question: What experiences should I prioritize before I start applying for internships? Like classes, research, clubs, personal projects, internships, leadership, networking, etc.
answers.answer: Basic finance classes are helpful. Networking is good. Have some kind of experience on your resume (even if it is just research) and be ready to motivate why you're interested in finance despite coming from an engineering school

answers.question: For someone from MIT, what opportunities or resources do you think I should take advantage of that students often overlook?
answers.answer: Taking classes at Sloan in accounting, corporate finance, etc. Easy As and not all undergraduates have access to business school classes

answers.question: What does a really strong candidate for an internship in your industry look like?
answers.answer: Relevant experience in finance or demonstrated knowledge in the industry. Very polished answers to behavioral and technical questions (from lots of interview prep). Also just being a normal person who is easy to talk to and that people want to work with

answers.question: What skills are actually important once you're working in the industry versus skills that are mostly useful for getting through the interview process?
answers.answer: You learn a ton on the job. There isn't really a way to prepare to spread comps nor do you need to know this while you're interviewing. Having knowledge of basic accounting and corporate finance is really all you need (don't just memorize answers to interview questions, you should actually understand what you're talking about)

answers.question: How did you get your first real opportunity in the industry?
answers.answer: Genuinely butterfly effect. The more people I talked to, the more doors opened that I didn't even realize existed. For example, I applied to Girls Who Invest after I talked to a recent rowing alum who works in private equity. GWI then matched me with an internship for my sophomore summer (an amazing opportunity). I do not like networking at face value and I only reach out to people that I genuinely want to connect with/am not just trying to get a referral from (and I think people respect this)

answers.question: When should I start recruiting, and what does the recruiting timeline look like for internships and full-time roles?
answers.answer: Junior summer internships usually open late fall/winter of your sophomore year (very early so do your diligence over the summer). Full time role recruiting is spread out over your junior summer and senior fall depending on what you want (hopefully you are just going back to your junior summer job though!)

answers.question: Are there particular companies, roles, or types of internships you think are especially good starting points?
answers.answer: Really depends on the person and what type of finance role you want to work in. Would recommend talking to people at different firms to figure out the vibes

answers.question: Are there mistakes you see some students make when trying to break into this industry?
answers.answer: Don't be a bot, be your authentic self and trust that you will find a solid internship for your junior summer (freshman and sophomore summers really don't matter that much). And know that your first job is almost definitely not your last so keep an open mind!

answers.question: How would you recommend I spend my freshman summer if my ultimate goal is to end up in this field?
answers.answer: Do something you care about. Like research in a cool field. I worked for a non profit. Just something you can talk about, doesn't have to be related to finance

answers.question: Should I go to the career fair as a freshman? If so, how should I prepare? If not, should I, and what years?
answers.answer: Sure, it's fun to meet people and get merch. Probably won't get a job but you can talk to the same employers in the future and maybe they'll like that you remember them from a prior year. But FYI the career fair is not very finance focused at all

answers.question: How important are GPA, major, coursework, extracurriculars, projects, and previous internships when companies are evaluating students?
answers.answer: GPA is very important, I've heard it should be above 4.6 but higher is always better. Major doesn't matter as long as you know finance stuff. Previous internships are a plus but not required. I've also heard firms like college athletes if you have that as an extracurricular

answers.question: Was there anyone at MIT, like a professor, alum, organization, or career resource, who was particularly helpful to you?
answers.answer: Recent alum (classes of 2024, 2025, 2026) were amaze and I am so lucky to know these smart and ambitious women <3

answers.question: If you were a freshman at MIT again and knew you wanted to go into this industry, what would you do differently over the next three years?
answers.answer: I would practice Leetcode very early on, make lots of coding projects for a portfolio, and try to UROP in CSAIL. I'd also try to spread out some of the harder CS classes a little more.

answers.question: What classes were the most important for industry work? Were any classes really important in terms of appearing on your resume?
What did you do during college that actually mattered in getting your first job, and what ended up not mattering as much as you thought it would?
answers.answer: Grades didn't matter as much as I thought they would in applications (there are a few exceptions). Networking with MIT alumni was very helpful in getting my first job. Being able to pass coding tests is also very important.

answers.question: Were there any clubs that bolstered your resume, helped you make important connections, or really enhanced your knowledge about the industry?
answers.answer: Participating in hackathons looks good on resume and also gives you projects to talk about. Alumni networking is important, and besides career fairs some companies will have their own smaller events/presentations on campus where they specifically look to connect with MIT students. GE Vernova has a partnership with MIT and that's where I connected with my assignment leader for my first internship.

answers.question: What experiences should I prioritize before I start applying for internships? Like classes, research, clubs, personal projects, internships, leadership, networking, etc.
answers.answer: Projects for GitHub portfolio, coding skills (Leetcode), and networking. Use UROPS to have experience on resume (CSAIL or Media Lab are good). If you wanna go GTL during IAP you could gain experience teaching computer science while traveling abroad which is nice for resume and personal experience.

answers.question: For someone from MIT, what opportunities or resources do you think I should take advantage of that students often overlook?
answers.answer: Alumni network website, mit career page, UROPing

answers.question: What does a really strong candidate for an internship in your industry look like?
answers.answer: Good coding skills for technical tests, lots of project based experience in a portfolio you can share, Research/internship experience related to computer science and AI, participating/winning hackathons

answers.question: What skills are actually important once you're working in the industry versus skills that are mostly useful for getting through the interview process?
answers.answer: Coding tests are important for the interview but honestly not as relevant when you're in the actual job. Experience building things is more helpful.

answers.question: How did you get your first real opportunity in the industry?
answers.answer: UROPs and networking

answers.question: When should I start recruiting, and what does the recruiting timeline look like for internships and full-time roles?
answers.answer: Internships/ Research freshmen and sophomore summer are helpful, recruiting starts August-Fall going into your junior year for internships that would hopefully lead into full time roles

answers.question: Are there particular companies, roles, or types of internships you think are especially good starting points?
answers.answer: UROPs, smaller startup roles, MIT partnership companies, anywhere you may have personal connections.

answers.question: Are there mistakes you see some students make when trying to break into this industry?
answers.answer: Focusing too much on grades and not enough on coding skills and projects. Not using network to full potential.

answers.question: How would you recommend I spend my freshman summer if my ultimate goal is to end up in this field?
answers.answer: UROP, MISTI, or find an internship in a computer science role

answers.question: Should I go to the career fair as a freshman? If so, how should I prepare? If not, should I, and what years?
answers.answer: Yes you should go. There are some companies that look for underclassmen, but though not many. You can still learn about companies and connect with people as a freshman.

answers.question: How important are GPA, major, coursework, extracurriculars, projects, and previous internships when companies are evaluating students?
answers.answer: Major, projects, and internships are most important. GPA is less important for most companies (if you have a dream/target company, research what they look for in GPA)

answers.question: Was there anyone at MIT, like a professor, alum, organization, or career resource, who was particularly helpful to you?
answers.answer: Connecting with alumni is helpful

answers.question: If you were a freshman at MIT again and knew you wanted to go into this industry, what would you do differently over the next three years?
answers.answer: Explore more of the programs that MIT offers for development! I found out about the Sloan Healthcare Certificate late, and exploring that in Freshman spring and Sophomore fall would have balanced my schedule more. There are also startup accelerators within MIT (Delta V, HEALS R2E, etc) that have examples of interesting biotech startups on campus. They host events that are generally open for students! Reading newsletters is a good way to hear about these things, and I wish I did that more seriously earlier in my MIT career.

answers.question: What classes were the most important for industry work? Were any classes really important in terms of appearing on your resume?
answers.answer: I have gotten a lot of interest from my sloan healthcare certificate courses! Specifically the following courses: Economics and Analytics of Healthcare Industries (15.141), Principles and Practice of Drug Development (15.136), Healthcare Lab (15.777), Genetics (7.03), and Biochemistry (7.05). I felt that my in major classes helped a lot with technical knowledge and skill, and my UROP and Sloan classes helped to put that in practice with greater context.

answers.question: What did you do during college that actually mattered in getting your first job, and what ended up not mattering as much as you thought it would?
answers.answer: Something that definitely made a difference was networking! Saying yes to every coffee chat, interview, etc helps make so many connections. I also was able to get a spot in an Eli Lilly program from the career fair so definitely recommend that! My exact grades honestly didn't matter as much as I thought they would. I have never been asked in an interview about my specific academic performance.

answers.question: Were there any clubs that bolstered your resume, helped you make important connections, or really enhanced your knowledge about the industry?
answers.answer: Having a position in the sorority has given me a lot of leadership experience (and interview answers for questions about leadership)! Highly recommend getting involved in some way! Also joining the HSI Sloan Newsletter :)

answers.question: What experiences should I prioritize before I start applying for internships? Like classes, research, clubs, personal projects, internships, leadership, networking, etc.
answers.answer: For pharma, definitely research where you can have some ownership over your project. This is super important for grad school as well! Also networking and connecting with people at different companies- I have gotten to go on a couple industry tours through my network!

answers.question: For someone from MIT, what opportunities or resources do you think I should take advantage of that students often overlook?
answers.answer: Reading newsletters! They have so much information on them. Also the possibility of getting an internship from the career fair! I know a couple pharma companies that seriously recruit from the career fair.

answers.question: What does a really strong candidate for an internship in your industry look like?
answers.answer: Definitely understanding of science via research! I also think that having concrete reasons why you are excited about a specific disease state or research lab beyond finding the science cool is important to think about!

answers.question: What skills are actually important once you're working in the industry versus skills that are mostly useful for getting through the interview process?
answers.answer: Being curious and having the ability to ask questions is super important in both interviews and working in the industry. For the interview process, make sure you understand the science that you reference (from class or lab experience). When working, being able to network and hold your own in conversations with people that have PhDs in life science subjects is important.

answers.question: How did you get your first real opportunity in the industry?
answers.answer: Career fair! I talked to Eli Lilly and got a short internship there that I have referenced in every interview since!

answers.question: When should I start recruiting, and what does the recruiting timeline look like for internships and full-time roles?
answers.answer: I got the Eli Lilly short program after the career fair in Sophomore year and it took place over Sophomore year IAP. I then got an internship via MISTI UK at a biotech accelerator which I organized during soph spring. I am now going through recruiting for summer before senior year. Most open this fall (so junior fall), but I am prepping application answers! From there I have heard multiple people get return offers from their summer internships!

answers.question: Are there particular companies, roles, or types of internships you think are especially good starting points?
answers.answer: Definitely R&D interns at big pharma companies! Most have student talent networks you can join (Takeda, Genentech, Eli Lilly, etc) and have built undergraduate intern programs.

answers.question: How would you recommend I spend my freshman summer if my ultimate goal is to end up in this field?
answers.answer: I would say working in a lab or if you have industry connections trying to get a start on that early. I have been asked my research experience in every interview, and having a project that you can take ownership of because you dedicated a whole summer to that is very important.

answers.question: Should I go to the career fair as a freshman? If so, how should I prepare? If not, should I, and what years?
answers.answer: Definitely go! It is helpful to see what is out there. I don't know if any have programs for freshmen but even putting your name on their radar can help! Mainly just update your resume, and have a ready-to-go answer for a tell me about yourself, what are you interested in career wise, and why are you talking to *specific company name*. DEFINITELY GO SOPH AND JUNIOR FALL if you are interested in Eli Lilly! I know a couple other pharma companies are there but the only one I personally got a chance to talk to was Lilly.

answers.question: How important are GPA, major, coursework, extracurriculars, projects, and previous internships when companies are evaluating students?
answers.answer: I have never been asked about my GPA, and to be honest don't have a perfect 5.0. Generally try your best and I am sure you will be great! I think lab experience and life sciences major/coursework are the most important. If you have previous internships that will help too but everyone starts somewhere!

answers.question: Was there anyone at MIT, like a professor, alum, organization, or career resource, who was particularly helpful to you?
answers.answer: Older members of Aphi! My grandbig is working in the field I want to go into, so she has helped me a lot with interview prep and recruiting. Just ask around and someone will know someone who can help you!

answers.question: If you were a freshman at MIT again and knew you wanted to go into this industry, what would you do differently over the next three years?
answers.answer: I would push myself to take courses in areas tangential but not directly related to what I was interested in. Every single random learning experience brings more color and creativity to your mind and ability to be a creative researcher and person.

answers.question: What classes were the most important for industry work? Were any classes really important in terms of appearing on your resume?
answers.answer: If you are considering Course 20 - DO NOT TAKE 6.10OB!!!!! TAKE 20.260 (it's like ML for BE)!!!! fulfills the same requirement, taught by THEE founder of bioengineering, and a million times more relevant in todays climate for biology / bioE.

answers.question: What did you do during college that actually mattered in getting your first job, and what ended up not mattering as much as you thought it would?
answers.answer: I want to do grad school / research full-time after graduating - I haven't been in any clubs related to my career interests, and I don't regret it at all. It's way more important IMO to spend your free time doing things that hold deep personal and creative value.

answers.question: Were there any clubs that bolstered your resume, helped you make important connections, or really enhanced your knowledge about the industry?
answers.answer: Don't hate me but Aphi!!! Meeting alums during career panels and coffee chats REALLY helped me understand what options there were in the (relatively niche) career path I wanted to be in.

answers.question: For someone from MIT, what opportunities or resources do you think I should take advantage of that students often overlook?
answers.answer: UROPPPPP. everyone, regardless of department, should look at the ELX website just to see the crazy opportunities!!!

answers.question: What does a really strong candidate for an internship in your industry look like?
answers.answer: tons of research + creativity and grit in personally motivated or planned projects.

answers.question: What skills are actually important once you're working in the industry versus skills that are mostly useful for getting through the interview process?
answers.answer: being able to easily admit when you don't know something

answers.question: How did you get your first real opportunity in the industry?
answers.answer: my first UROP mentor connected me to his colleague at another research institute!

answers.question: Are there mistakes you see some students make when trying to break into this industry?
answers.answer: focusing too much on classes and not enough on research

answers.question: How would you recommend I spend my freshman summer if my ultimate goal is to end up in this field?
answers.answer: work with a well established professor and make an extremely positive impression with your desire to learn and dedication. freshman year is for doing the most! but also balancing work and friends.

answers.question: Should I go to the career fair as a freshman? If so, how should I prepare? If not, should I, and what years?
answers.answer: i went once and never again!!! But it depends on your field. look at the companies before going.

answers.question: If you were a freshman at MIT again and knew you wanted to go into this industry, what would you do differently over the next three years?
answers.answer: More focus on project work so that you feel confident in being able to make something on your own

answers.question: What classes were the most important for industry work? Were any classes really important in terms of appearing on your resume?
answers.answer: I think 6.1010 is super good just so you understand basic code since a lot of course 2A classes also require basic coding - it makes things a lot easier to pick up. 2.007 is super cool, there are mixed reviews on 2.12 but I personally thought it was really worthwhile.

answers.question: What did you do during college that actually mattered in getting your first job, and what ended up not mattering as much as you thought it would?
answers.answer: Haven't gotten first full time job...but from my understanding it seems like GPA doesn't matter QUITE as much and it's more focused on coursework/project work

answers.question: What experiences should I prioritize before I start applying for internships? Like classes, research, clubs, personal projects, internships, leadership, networking, etc.
answers.answer: Research, personal projects, internships

answers.question: For someone from MIT, what opportunities or resources do you think I should take advantage of that students often overlook?
answers.answer: Talking to your professors -- I definitely should have taken the time to get to know my instructors better because most of the time, they are involved in some of the coolest research ever outside of teaching classes

answers.question: What does a really strong candidate for an internship in your industry look like?
answers.answer: CAD, FEA, Arudino, Python, C++, experience using skills in project work

answers.question: What skills are actually important once you're working in the industry versus skills that are mostly useful for getting through the interview process?
answers.answer: Really depends on your role - I've seen some people whose entire role revolves around doing CAD and/or FEA, but sometimes you're left to just learn something on your own later. Just be adaptable!

answers.question: How did you get your first real opportunity in the industry?
answers.answer: MISTI, then the following year was a referral from a sister!

answers.question: When should I start recruiting, and what does the recruiting timeline look like for internships and full-time roles?
answers.answer: For MechE probably around August/September for the following summer for tech internships like Google, Apple, etc. but many companies like GE Vernova and/or smaller companies continue hiring through spring of the following year

answers.question: How would you recommend I spend my freshman summer if my ultimate goal is to end up in this field?
answers.answer: Startup (if that's something you're interested in), UROP at MIT, or spend the summer working on a personal project to learn something new

answers.question: Should I go to the career fair as a freshman? If so, how should I prepare? If not, should I, and what years?
answers.answer: Yes, but don't go in with any expectations. Just look at the companies and watch what the older students do.

answers.question: How important are GPA, major, coursework, extracurriculars, projects, and previous internships when companies are evaluating students?
answers.answer: GPA - meh I think? Major is a big one because I think it ties into coursework (especially for something like mech e where you wouldn't really learn CAD skills and some foundational skills unless you were a course 2 or 2A). Extracurriculars CAN be helpful but not always, depends what you do (they love things like MIT Motorsports and Rocket Team and whatnot but I personally never did them because of the huge time commitment). Previous internships...not sure, sorry.

answers.question: If you were a freshman at MIT again and knew you wanted to go into this industry, what would you do differently over the next three years?
answers.answer: Network!!!!! Become a LinkedIn warrior and just talk to as many people as you possibly can. Don't be afraid to reach out to anyone and just be yourself in your convos

answers.question: What classes were the most important for industry work? Were any classes really important in terms of appearing on your resume?
answers.answer: 6.102 and 6.1210 for swe interviews, I lovedddd GEL classes to help me work on soft skills

answers.question: What did you do during college that actually mattered in getting your first job, and what ended up not mattering as much as you thought it would?
answers.answer: Talking to people and getting referrals was pretty helpful, I learned a lot from failing at things too (dreading swe interviews helped me learn that I don't want to work in that role)

answers.question: Were there any clubs that bolstered your resume, helped you make important connections, or really enhanced your knowledge about the industry?
answers.answer: MITxHarvard Women in AI (amazing buzzwords) and Student Events Board gave me lots of leadership and teamwork examples

answers.question: What experiences should I prioritize before I start applying for internships? Like classes, research, clubs, personal projects, internships, leadership, networking, etc.
answers.answer: Internships are fun to learn what you like and dislike, urops are soooo helpful to have something on your resume to land those

answers.question: For someone from MIT, what opportunities or resources do you think I should take advantage of that students often overlook?
answers.answer: MIT's name opens soooo many doors so talk to as many people as you can. CAPD was pretty helpful in giving me confidence going into spring career fair and that's how I landed my junior summer internship. It's never too late to find something to do over the summer

answers.question: What does a really strong candidate for an internship in your industry look like?
answers.answer: Curious, leader, bold thinking, creative, personable

answers.question: What skills are actually important once you're working in the industry versus skills that are mostly useful for getting through the interview process?
answers.answer: Asking questions when you're stuck is so helpful in industry

answers.question: How did you get your first real opportunity in the industry?
answers.answer: MIT spring career fair and networking events

answers.question: When should I start recruiting, and what does the recruiting timeline look like for internships and full-time roles?
answers.answer: Honestly end of summer through fall of the year before, but don't stress bc there are still opportunities in the spring

answers.question: Are there particular companies, roles, or types of internships you think are especially good starting points?

answers.question: If you were a freshman at MIT again and knew you wanted to go into this industry, what would you do differently over the next three years?
answers.answer:
Start personal projects that teach you the skills you want to know. You need something? Build an app for it. You wish something was better? Make it, but better.
Often times the skills you need won't necessarily be taught in your classes, so you might need to go and seek them out.

answers.question: What classes were the most important for industry work? Were any classes really important in terms of appearing on your resume?
answers.answer:
6.UAT, 6.390, 6.1210, 18.06. Each of those are super important day to day.
I've never been asked about my coursework listed on my resume unless I brought it up as an answer to an interview question

answers.question: What did you do during college that actually mattered in getting your first job, and what ended up not mattering as much as you thought it would?
answers.answer:
BEING ABLE TO TALK ABOUT THE COOL THINGS YOUVE DONE.
You might have built something really cool but no one is going to care if you can't explain it in a way that is understandable and impressive. Sure, the things I did in undergrad like internships and research are cool, but they only meant something to people interviewing me because I made them sound cool. You need to be able to explain technical concepts to varying audiences. Using big words and jargon is much less impressive than explaining something complicated in a very concise way. No matter what you do, practice talking about it and telling a story about it.

answers.question: Were there any clubs that bolstered your resume, helped you make important connections, or really enhanced your knowledge about the industry?
answers.answer: None stood out. I think the most important thing for network is making a genuine connection, and that's definitely easier when you have something in common. I found that extracurriculars were most useful for finding that common ground, especially with younger people I was networking with.

answers.question: What experiences should I prioritize before I start applying for internships? Like classes, research, clubs, personal projects, internships, leadership, networking, etc.
answers.answer: 1. Internships, 2. Personal projects, 3. Leadership probably. Depending on what sort of role you want. No matter what you do, make sure it is something you are actually passionate about. Don't do something just because you think it will look good, do something because you want to!

answers.question: For someone from MIT, what opportunities or resources do you think I should take advantage of that students often overlook?
answers.answer: PKG Center. I got my first internship with them, and I did it over IAP. I got a 2 thousand dollar stipend for the month and some pretty great work experience that I still bring up during interviews. The people there are lovely and internships with them are (in my experience) a bit easier to get. Also all of their internships have some sort of social impact connection which rocks. Highly recommend

answers.question: What does a really strong candidate for an internship in your industry look like?
answers.answer: Someone with hands on experience through internships, personal projects, and research. Someone who is driven and a great communicator (many CS people are bad at talking, you probably aren't!). Personal projects can really set you apart.

answers.question: What skills are actually important once you're working in the industry versus skills that are mostly useful for getting through the interview process?
answers.answer:
Industry - being self motivated, coding with AI, test driven development (making unit tests, etc.), presenting, writing
Interviews - explaining why you are cool and unique, coding without AI, fast problem solving, algorithms knowledge

answers.question: How did you get your first real opportunity in the industry?
answers.answer: Cold emailing UROPS got me my first experience with full stack development. From their, I got and internship through the PKG center Indigenous Communities Initiative, and then through MISTI. My first internship that wasn't through an MIT program was my summer between Junior and Senior year. For that summer, I probably applied to about 150 jobs and only got 2 offers. Rejection sucks but is apart of the process! It's gonna be okay I swear, just keep trying

answers.question: When should I start recruiting, and what does the recruiting timeline look like for internships and full-time roles?
answers.answer: Every company is different, but a lot of SWE summer internships for big name companies are posted in early August. Some companies are much later, especially startups. A good time to start recruiting is in the fall, but if you start after that it's totally okay.

answers.question: Are there particular companies, roles, or types of internships you think are especially good starting points?
answers.answer: Depends on what you want! Often times big companies have more opportunities for mentorship and structured learning, but startups let you wear many hats.

answers.question: Are there mistakes you see some students make when trying to break into this industry?
answers.answer: Thinking that you have to go to a big name company to be successful. Focus less on what you think would impress others and more on what you think you would actually like. Internships and early jobs are all about learning and exploring, so prioritize that.

answers.question: How would you recommend I spend my freshman summer if my ultimate goal is to end up in this field?
answers.answer: Maybe find a fun little side project! Freshman summer is definitely not make or break but it could be a good opportunity to set yourself apart. Have fun though, school is hard enough. Don't go too hard in the early summers or you will burn out.

answers.question: Should I go to the career fair as a freshman? If so, how should I prepare? If not, should I, and what years?
answers.answer:
Hell no. If you do, just grab merch and get out. If you REALLY want to do the career fair, use it as practice pitching yourself. Lots of companies are not looking for freshman, so the career fair could be a good chance to practice rejection! 
If you really want to get a job at the career fair my advice is to research the companies beforehand, make a list of who you want to talk to with targeted questions, print out your resume, and practice an elevator pitch.

answers.question: How important are GPA, major, coursework, extracurriculars, projects, and previous internships when companies are evaluating students?
answers.answer:
GPA not too much. It certainly doesn't hurt to have a good GPA but mine isn't great and I've never been asked about it.
Major, not at all as long as you've had relevant experiences to the role.
Coursework, sort of. 
Extracurriculars, if you have something impressive it helps but otherwise not that important. 
Previous internships and projects are most important.

answers.question: Was there anyone at MIT, like a professor, alum, organization, or career resource, who was particularly helpful to you?
answers.answer: Aphi upperclassmen. PLEASE bother upperclassmen with your questions - we were helped by upperclassmen and we want to pay it forward.
